subject: maths
title: GCSE Maths diagnostic
curriculum: DfE GCSE mathematics subject content (2013), shared by AQA, Edexcel, OCR and WJEC. Also suitable for IGCSE.

skills.name: Number and calculation
skills.why: Confident calculation sits underneath every GCSE topic and saves marks on every paper.
skills.strong: {name} calculates accurately and handles primes and powers with confidence.
skills.developing: {name} is secure with everyday calculation but less sure with prime factors and powers.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with the order of operations and number facts. Small slips here cost marks across the whole paper, so it is worth fixing first.
skills.next_step: We will tighten up calculation habits with short, regular practice.

skills.name: Fractions, decimals and percentages
skills.why: Fractions and percentages appear all over GCSE, from probability to money problems.
skills.strong: {name} moves easily between fractions, decimals and percentages, including reverse percentages.
skills.developing: {name} handles simple conversions well but finds adding fractions and reverse percentages harder.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident working with fractions and percentages. These come up on almost every paper, so they are worth securing now.
skills.next_step: We will rebuild this step by step, from equivalent fractions to percentage change.

skills.name: Ratio and proportion
skills.why: Ratio and proportion carry a large share of GCSE marks and link maths to real life.
skills.strong: {name} works confidently with ratio, proportion and compound interest.
skills.developing: {name} can simplify and share in a ratio but is less sure with proportion and growth.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident sharing in a ratio or working with proportion. This is a big part of the GCSE, so it is worth tackling early.
skills.next_step: We will use bar models and real examples to make ratio feel concrete.

skills.name: Algebra
skills.why: Algebra is the biggest single area of GCSE maths and the key to the higher grades.
skills.strong: {name} solves equations, factorises and handles simultaneous equations well.
skills.developing: {name} can solve simple equations and expand brackets but finds factorising and simultaneous equations harder.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with the basics of algebra. So much of the GCSE builds on this that it should come first.
skills.next_step: We will build algebra up from solving one-step equations, with lots of worked examples.

skills.name: Geometry and measures
skills.why: Geometry questions reward clear methods, so secure skills here turn into reliable marks.
skills.strong: {name} uses Pythagoras, trigonometry and scale factors confidently.
skills.developing: {name} is secure with area and Pythagoras but less sure with trigonometry and similar shapes.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with area and right-angled triangles. These methods come up every year, so they are worth securing.
skills.next_step: We will practise the key formulas and when to use each one.

skills.name: Probability and statistics
skills.why: Statistics and probability questions are often the most accessible marks on the paper.
skills.strong: {name} works confidently with averages and probability, including combined events.
skills.developing: {name} handles averages and single events well but finds combined probability harder.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident with averages and probability. These are some of the easiest marks to gain, so they are a quick win.
skills.next_step: We will work through averages and probability with short, clear methods.

questions.stem: Work out 3 + 4 × 5
questions.explain: Multiply first: 4 × 5 = 20, then 3 + 20 = 23. 35 comes from working left to right.

questions.stem: What is 1/4 as a percentage?
questions.explain: 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. 14% comes from reading the digits 1 and 4.

questions.stem:
Solve 3x + 5 = 20

What is the value of x?
A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. What is its area?
questions.explain: 8 × 5 = 40 cm². 26 would be the perimeter.

questions.stem:
Find the median of these numbers:
3, 9, 7, 4, 2
questions.explain: In order: 2, 3, 4, 7, 9. The middle value is 4. 7 is the middle before ordering; 5 is the mean.

questions.stem: Write the ratio 12 : 18 in its simplest form.
questions.explain: Divide both by 6: 2 : 3. 6 : 9 and 4 : 6 are equivalent but not simplest; 3 : 2 is reversed.

questions.stem: Expand 4(2x − 3)
questions.explain: 4 × 2x = 8x and 4 × −3 = −12. 8x − 3 forgets to multiply the second term.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided dice is rolled. What is the probability of rolling a number greater than 4?
questions.explain: Greater than 4 means 5 or 6: 2 out of 6 = 1/3. 1/6 counts only one outcome; 1/2 includes 4.

questions.stem: £40 is shared in the ratio 3 : 5. How much is the larger share?
questions.explain: 8 parts, so 1 part = £5. The larger share is 5 × £5 = £25.

questions.stem: Write 360 as a product of its prime factors.
questions.explain: 360 = 8 × 45 = 2³ × 3² × 5. Every option multiplies to 360, but only D uses primes only.

questions.stem: Work out 2/3 + 1/4
questions.explain: 2/3 = 8/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so 11/12. 3/7 adds tops and bottoms.

questions.stem: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides of 6 cm and 8 cm. How long is the hypotenuse?
questions.explain: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100, and √100 = 10 cm. 14 comes from adding the sides.

questions.stem: Factorise x² + 7x + 12
questions.explain: Need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7: 3 and 4. (x + 2)(x + 6) multiplies to 12 but adds to 8.

questions.stem: The mean of four numbers is 12. Three of the numbers are 10, 15 and 9. What is the fourth number?
In a sale, a laptop costs £450 after a 25% reduction. What was the original price?
questions.explain: £450 is 75% of the original, so original = 450 ÷ 0.75 = £600. £562.50 comes from adding 25% of £450.

questions.stem: y is directly proportional to x. When x = 4, y = 10. What is y when x = 10?
questions.explain: y = 2.5x, so when x = 10, y = 25. 16 adds 6 to both; 40 multiplies 4 by 10.

questions.stem:
In a right-angled triangle, the side opposite angle x is 7 cm and the hypotenuse is 14 cm.

What is the size of angle x?

Solve these simultaneous equations:
2x + y = 11
x − y = 1

What is the value of x?
questions.explain: Adding the equations gives 3x = 12, so x = 4 (and y = 3). Check: 8 + 3 = 11 and 4 − 3 = 1.

questions.stem:
A bag holds 3 red counters and 5 blue counters. Two counters are taken out at random, without replacement.

What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explain: 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28. 9/64 assumes the first counter is put back.

questions.stem: £2000 is invested at 3% compound interest per year. How much is it worth after 2 years? Give your answer to the nearest penny.
What is the value of 8 to the power of 2/3?
questions.explain: Cube root of 8 is 2, and 2² = 4. 16/3 multiplies 8 by 2/3; 2 stops after the cube root.

questions.stem:
Two cylinders are mathematically similar. Their heights are 4 cm and 12 cm. The smaller cylinder has a volume of 20 cm³.

What is the volume of the larger cylinder?
questions.explain: Length scale factor 3, so volume scale factor 3³ = 27. 20 × 27 = 540 cm³. 60 uses 3 and 180 uses 3² = 9.
